purpose: Lansoprazole is used to reduce the amount of acid your stomach makes. It helps treat conditions like heartburn, acid reflux, stomach ulcers, and a condition called GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease). It can also help protect your stomach when you take certain pain medicines like ibuprofen.
how_it_works: Your stomach has tiny pumps that produce acid to help digest food. Lansoprazole works by blocking these pumps so they make much less acid. With less acid, your stomach and food pipe (esophagus) get a chance to heal and stop hurting.
common_side_effects: Most people tolerate this medicine well, but some may notice headache, diarrhea, nausea, stomach pain, or constipation. These are usually mild and go away on their own.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have low magnesium levels, liver problems, or osteoporosis (weak bones), as long-term use can affect these. Taking this medicine for a long time may slightly increase the risk of bone fractures, low magnesium, or a gut infection called C. difficile. Always let your doctor know all the medicines you take, as lansoprazole can interact with some medications like methotrexate or certain HIV medicines.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 15 mg to 30 mg taken once a day, usually in the morning before eating. Your doctor will tell you the right dose and how long to take it — some people only need a few weeks, while others may need longer treatment.
